items.content:
RT @pavelsimo: Day 24/100 of Inference Engineering

> today i finished chapter 7 of inference engineering: section 7.5: client code, the last chapter of the book.... 

> great learnings so far! tomorrow we continue with the next "quest", stay around! :)

> a lot of "tech" is going into making inference engineering work... cuda, kubernetes, vLLM, etc. but one thing is often overlooked is client code.

> what do we mean by "client code"? well, for inference to happen, your computer has to be able to reach the server where the model is hosted, so a request has to go from your machine to that server.

> there's nothing magical about this. it's a typical client-server model: your machine is the client, and the inference service is the server.

> the openai sdk is a popular choice for sending requests to a inference service. you can also use libraries like langchain, vercel ai sdk, litellm or llamaindex.

> the book explains that setting up an https connection requires a tls handshake, which adds significant latency... the way to go here is to reuse the session and avoid repeating the tls handshake for each request.

> the openai sdk handles this under the hood, but if you're building your own custom http client make sure you're not doing repeated tls handshakes...

> keep in mind, "http" is not always the way to go... for real-time apps you might want to keep a connection open so the client and server can keep exchanging messages... websockets are nice option for this.

> if you're processing lots of documents and don't need results right away, async jobs make a lot of sense... this usually means your workload is optimize for throughput, whenever you identify this pattern think async...

> an async request is a "fire and forget" kind of thing... the way this is usually implemented is a follow: the client sends a request, the server acknowledges the job, then sends the results back via a webhook when they're ready.

> finally, streaming is a nice way to make your app feel "responsive"...

> for text output, http usually works pretty well... unless you have really "special" requirements.

> for other modalities like video and audio, it's better to reach for something more "fancy" like websockets or grpc :)

> websockets and grpc create a bidirectional connection between the client and server, where both sides can send messages as long as the connection stays open.

> pick websockets when you're sending unstructured and real-time data, like audio.

> pick grpc when you’re dealing with structured data: requests sent via grpc must follow a predefined schema. that schema thing is not "free", it involves parsing... so it adds some overhead to the comunication.

MIT researchers (Joseph Ravichandran and Mengjia Yan) built Fractal, an operating system kernel designed entirely for microarchitecture reverse engineering. Using it, they discovered previously undocumented behaviors in Apple's M1 processor including instruction cache side channels and the first evidence that Phantom speculation affects Apple Silicon. 

In Phantom, ordinary instructions including no-ops can be misinterpreted by the CPU as branches, triggering speculative behavior the program never asked for. The CPU still fetches the target into the instruction cache before the protection kicks in.

RT @WindowsLatest: This is Windows 11's new native Search, and it's finally rolling out.

I've been testing Windows 11's completely rebuilt Search, and it's easily one of my favourite changes Microsoft has made to the OS this year!

Microsoft has finally ditched the WebView2-based interface in favour of native WinUI 3, and the difference is immediately noticeable.

You will notice that Search now opens faster, typing feels smoother, and uses around 15–20% less RAM. Some other features:

- Inline actions: Change brightness, enable Bluetooth, switch to dark mode, mute your PC, and more, directly from Search.
- One results list: No more oversized preview pane wasting screen space.
- Better file search: Richer previews, file details, typo correction, and synonyms.
- Phone integration: Call contacts, send texts, and access phone actions through Phone Link.

I particularly love the inline actions, and here's a video showing them off. Look how I can now adjust my PC's brightness without even opening Settings!

Windows Search is finally becoming something genuinely useful instead of just another place to find apps and files.

I've also tested the new experience on Windows 11 26H2, and it's remarkably smooth.

items.content:
RT @make_claude: Rockstar Games 周三解雇了我。第二天 GTA 6 就发售了

我是 Rockstar North 的高级引擎工程师，从事 RAGE 性能优化。三个月前，我在遥测模块里发现了一条本不该存在的数据管道，而且我能证明它流向了哪里

此刻每一份正在运行的 GTA 6 都在收集玩家的行为数据。这部分不算新闻。每款游戏都会收集遥测数据。隐私政策里写的是"用于改进未来产品的匿名游戏数据分析"。我发现的不是这个

遥测模块的数据会汇入 Take-Two 内部的一个系统，名为 Lens。Lens 并不会把匿名使用统计数据发送到 Rockstar 开发人员的数据看板。它为每一位玩家建立一份个人行为画像。不是匿名的。与你的主机账号、你的平台 ID、你的 IP 绑定

我在8月14日向我的技术主管报告了这件事。他说这是"用于玩家体验研究的扩展分析"，让我别管这事。我要求提供数据处理协议。他说这是在 Take-Two 集团层面处理的，不在 Rockstar 的职责范围之内

我调取了 Lens 数据管道的完整文档。我发现的内容如下：

遥测的内容远远超出游戏时长和崩溃报告。Lens 以毫秒级精度记录每一次输入。按键时间点、摇杆动作、反应速度、PS5 自适应扳机上的扳机压力模式。它实时运行行为分析，并生成他们称之为"玩家行为签名"的东西 - 一份对每位玩家都独一无二的画像，就像指纹对每个人都独一无二一样

Lens 会从你的游戏过程中推导出：冲动控制评分、风险承受度指数、攻击性反应模式、耐心阈值、压力下的决策速度、消费冲动评级。这些不是调试指标。这些是心理行为类别

直到我找到了对外传输的管道，我才明白它们是用来做什么的

这些数据不会留在 Rockstar。也不会留在 Take-Two。Lens 通过内部 API 将行为画像传送给 Take-Two 旗下一家名为 Vantage Analytics 的子公司。Vantage 没有公开网站，没有新闻页面，没有招聘信息。它于2023年在特拉华州注册成立

Vantage 是一家行为 AI 公司。它用玩家画像训练预测模型，并把这些模型授权给商业客户。管道文档中包含一份不完整的客户清单。两家保险集团，一家信用风险建模公司，一个人力资源筛选平台，以及一家广告数据经纪商

你的 GTA 6 游戏过程此刻正在生成一份行为评分。没人追你的时候，你开得有多快。你会不会在红灯前停下。NPC 无端攻击你时，你怎么反应。你行动之前要想多久。你花游戏内的钱有多冲动。每一个选择都在喂养一个模型，企业正在付费查询这个模型，用来对真实的人做决定

items.content:
RT @0xpwnie: New lecture on pwncollege, presented by guest lecturer Jennifer Miller (Zolutal) from the SEPCOM lab, provides an introduction to Linux kernel security and exploitation concepts within the context of the CSE466 course (0:00-0:15).

Key takeaways from the lecture:

> Kernel Basics: The kernel acts as the interface between hardware and userland applications, handling task scheduling and interprocess communication (1:08-1:36).

> Kernel Modules: These are extensions to the kernel, ranging from drivers to security modules. They can be in-tree (part of the kernel source) or out-of-tree (proprietary/external) (2:46-3:51).
Interacting with Modules: The lecture demonstrates how modules expose functionality to user space, specifically through `/proc` entries and the `ioctl` system call (3:51-6:07).

Exploitation Concepts:
> Privilege Escalation: A primary goal, often involving the manipulation of the `task_struct` and `cred` structures to set the effective UID to 0 (root) (11:03-13:09).

> Memory Protections: Discusses mitigations like KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization), which randomizes memory positions (15:08-16:00).

> Kernel Shellcoding: Unlike user space, kernel shellcode calls internal kernel functions directly. The lecture demonstrates allocating RWX (Read-Write-Execute) memory pages and triggering execution through a modified kernel module (8:51-11:03, 42:00-58:50).

> Debugging: The lecture provides practical guidance on using GDB to interact with the guest kernel, noting the challenges of debugging with hardware-assisted virtualization and the benefits of using emulator mode (7:55-8:41, 51:42-55:17).
